plants.name: Colchicum autumnale
plants.description: In damp meadows, bare pink-lilac goblets push straight out of the ground, with no leaves around them. They look like crocuses that have lost their way. The foliage only appears the following spring.
plants.bloomingSeason: September to October, which includes September 19
plants.location: Meadows and grasslands across central and western Europe
plants.funFact: Despite the name, it is not a true crocus. It belongs to the lily family and contains colchicine, a toxic compound. Plant breeders use colchicine to double the chromosomes of other plants.

plants.name: Acacia pycnantha
plants.description: Australia's national floral emblem covers itself in fluffy, fragrant golden pom-poms in the southern spring. Each ball is a cluster of 40 to 80 tiny flowers. Whole hillsides glow gold.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late August to September, which covers September 19
plants.location: Southeastern Australia, including South Australia, Victoria and New South Wales
plants.funFact: Australians celebrate National Wattle Day on September 1. In full bloom the tree displays the green and gold of the country's national colours.

plants.name: Solidago canadensis
plants.description: Tall stems carry arching plumes of tiny golden flowers. Bees, butterflies and beetles crowd onto them in the late-summer sun. It lights up roadsides, prairies and meadows as autumn approaches.
plants.bloomingSeason: August to October, which includes September 19
plants.location: Eastern and central North America, from Canada to the central United States
plants.funFact: Goldenrod is often blamed for hay fever, but its pollen is heavy and sticky and travels by insect. Ragweed, which blooms at the same time, is usually the real culprit.

plants.name: Lycoris radiata
plants.description: Leafless stalks shoot up almost overnight. Each is topped with a crown of crimson flowers whose long, curling stamens look like spider legs. In Japan, rice-field edges and riverbanks flush red around the autumn equinox.
plants.bloomingSeason: Around September, peaking near the autumn equinox, which covers September 19
plants.location: Japan, plus gardens in China, Korea and the southeastern United States
plants.funFact: The Japanese name higanbana refers to the equinox week of Higan, when the flowers appear. They are traditionally planted around rice paddies and graveyards because the bulbs are toxic to rodents and other pests.
